segments.text: [style: brisk, clear, architectural voice; steady studio cadence] Book Three, Proposition Twenty-Three. On the same segment, and on the same side of it, there cannot be constructed two similar and unequal segments of circles. For, if possible, on the same segment A B and on the same side, let two similar and unequal circle segments A C B and A D B be constructed.

segments.text: [style: luminous, deductive geometric clarity] Because circle segment A C B is similar to circle segment A D B, and by Book Three, Definition Eleven similar segments of circles are those which admit equal angles, the inscribed angle A C B equals the inscribed angle A D B. Yet in triangle C D B, angle A C B is an exterior angle and angle A D B is its opposite interior angle; so an exterior angle equals an opposite interior angle, which is impossible by One Sixteen. Therefore, on the same segment and on the same side, two similar and unequal circle segments cannot be constructed, as was required to prove.

segments.text: [style: reflective, scholarly, architectural synthesis] Proposition Twenty-Three is the circular counterpart of Book One, Proposition Seven: just as side lengths uniquely rigidify a triangle on a base, the inscribed angle uniquely determines the circle segment on a chord. As Robert Simson noted in Heath's commentary, because the two circles already intersect at A and B, Three Ten guarantees they cannot cross again—forcing one arc wholly inside the other and setting up the exterior-angle contradiction of One Sixteen. In the GEOMETOR G-Index, node G one hundred twenty-eight synthesizes forty ancestor nodes, bridging Definition Eleven's similar circle segments with Book One's exterior angle inequality.
